common_name: Winter Banana Apple (Aromatic Banana-Scented Indiana Heirloom)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Winter Banana produces little viable pollen of its own and is best planted alongside two compatible pollinizer varieties, and is well adapted to zones 4-8.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, with two different compatible pollinizer varieties nearby. Winter Banana was discovered in Indiana in 1876 and takes its name from a genuinely distinctive banana-like aroma and subtle fruity flavor note unlike any other common apple, carried in pale waxy-yellow skin blushed with soft pink to rose-red. The tender, crisp, aromatic flesh is best for fresh eating, where its unusual fragrance and flavor are most appreciated, and it also has a long history of use as a pollinizer tree for other apple varieties despite producing little viable pollen itself, thanks to its extended, reliable bloom period. Fruit ripens in fall and keeps reasonably well in cool storage, though its main appeal remains the striking aroma that makes it a memorable, conversation-starting addition to a home orchard.

common_name: Fameuse Apple (Snow Apple, French-Canadian Heirloom with Pure White Flesh)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; very cold-hardy and best adapted to zones 3-7, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Fameuse, commonly called the Snow Apple for its strikingly pure white flesh, traces back to French settlers in what is now Quebec in the 1600s, making it one of the oldest apple varieties associated with North American cultivation, and it is widely believed to be a parent of the famous McIntosh. The small to medium fruit has deep red, sometimes nearly crimson skin over snow-white flesh that is tender, juicy, and aromatic with a mild, sweet-tart flavor, best enjoyed fresh rather than cooked, since the delicate flesh breaks down quickly with heat. The tree is exceptionally cold-hardy, reflecting its origins in the harsh climate of early Quebec, and fruit ripens in fall but does not keep especially long, so it is best used within a couple of months of harvest.

common_name: Chenango Strawberry Apple (Delicate Strawberry-Scented New York Heirloom)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; best adapted to zones 4-7, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Chenango Strawberry originated in Chenango County, New York in the early 1800s, prized for its distinctive elongated, conical shape and delicate strawberry-like aroma and flavor note that gives it its evocative name — a subtlety not found in most other apple varieties. The thin, red-striped skin covers pale, tender, juicy flesh that is best appreciated fresh, since the delicate texture and short storage life make it poorly suited to long keeping or heavy cooking. Grown today mainly by heirloom orchardists and collectors for its unusual character and history rather than commercial reliability, it rewards patient home growers with a genuinely distinctive eating experience unlike common modern apples. Harvest in late summer to early fall and use fairly promptly, since the fruit softens quickly off the tree.

Smokehouse originated in Lancaster County, Pennsylvania in the early 1800s, reportedly discovered as a seedling growing near a farm smokehouse, and it became a widely planted, dependable all-purpose apple across the Mid-Atlantic for over a century. The medium to large fruit has yellow skin streaked and blushed with red, and the crisp, firm, juicy flesh carries a well-balanced sweet-tart flavor that performs equally well fresh, baked, and pressed for cider, a genuine multipurpose apple in the old farmstead tradition. The vigorous, productive tree bears reliably and holds fruit reasonably well in storage, making it a solid choice for home orchardists who want a historic variety without the finicky habits of some rarer heirlooms.

Summer Rambo, also known by its original French name Rambour, dates to at least the 1500s in France, making it one of the oldest apple varieties still in cultivation today and a variety that traveled to North America with some of the earliest European settlers. The large, somewhat flattened fruit has pale greenish-yellow skin streaked with red, and the crisp, juicy, notably tart flesh cooks down quickly into excellent sauce and is well suited to pies and other baked goods, though it can also be eaten fresh by those who favor a sharper apple. True to its ancient origins as a working farm variety, the tree is vigorous, disease-tolerant, and reliably productive; fruit ripens in mid to late summer, well ahead of most fall storage apples, and should be used within a few weeks since it does not keep long.
